title: DT: Cycling a Barbell Without Burning Out
excerpt: DT is five rounds of deadlifts, hang power cleans, and push jerks with one barbell. How to pace it, keep the bar cycling, and scale the weight so your grip and shoulders last.
description: DT is five rounds of deadlifts, hang power cleans, and push jerks with one barbell. How to pace it, keep the bar moving, and scale the weight so your grip and shoulders last.

toc.title: What DT Actually Asks of You
Pace the Rounds, Not the Reps
Choosing a Weight You Can Finish With

bodyHtml:
One Barbell, Three Lifts

DT is a hero workout, named in memory of a fallen service member, and it looks almost too simple on paper. Five rounds of 12 deadlifts, 9 hang power cleans, and 6 push jerks, all with the same barbell. Rx is 155 pounds for men and 105 for women. You never put the bar down for long, never change plates, and never get to walk away from it.

That is exactly why people get fooled. The weight is not heavy for most trained athletes. The trouble is that the bar stays in your hands, your grip never fully recovers, and the shoulders carry 30 touches of overhead work by the end. A lot of DT attempts are lost on round four, not round one.

"DT is not won in the first round. It is won by the athlete whose round five looks like round two."

What DT Actually Asks of You

Each round is 27 reps across three different patterns: a hip hinge off the floor, a quick pull from the hang position, and a dip-and-drive overhead. Add it up and you have 60 deadlifts, 45 hang power cleans, and 30 push jerks. Sub-20 minutes is a strong time, and most athletes land somewhere between 15 and 30.

The deadlifts are your volume, the cleans are your connector, and the push jerks are where the shoulders start to talk. Notice that none of the three is a long grind. They are short sets you can nearly always do unbroken, which tempts you to go out fast. Resist it. The workout is a test of how well you can keep repeating a clean lift when your forearms are cooked.

You can find the full movement list and Rx weights on the DT workout page, and the three lifts each have their own page: deadlifts, hang power cleans, and push jerks.

Pace the Rounds, Not the Reps

Aim for rounds that take roughly the same amount of time. If your first round takes 2:30 and your fifth takes 5:00, you spent your effort in the wrong place. A steadier athlete who runs 3:30, 3:35, 3:40, 3:45, 3:50 finishes ahead of the one who sprints round one and then hangs on.

A simple approach: do the deadlifts as one unbroken set, move to the cleans without a pause, and break the push jerks only if you must, with a planned rest of a few breaths rather than a wander around the garage. Plan one short break per round at most. Where you take it matters. Most people do best breaking after the cleans, because that is the cheapest moment to reset grip before the overhead work.

Grip check: If your hands are opening up during the deadlifts, you are going too fast for the weight. Slow the first two rounds down a touch. Chalk helps, and so does a hook grip you have already practiced, but test either one before the day you are racing the clock.

Keeping the Bar Cycling

Cycling a barbell means every rep flows into the next without a dead stop that costs you time and energy. Three small habits do most of the work.

First, treat the deadlift as a setup for the clean. Finish tall, lower the bar under control to the hang position at the knee, and start the first power clean from there instead of dropping to the floor again. Second, catch the clean high and quick, with elbows fast, so the bar lands in the front rack without crashing into your shoulders. Third, let the clean's rack position flow straight into the push jerk: a small dip, a hard drive, and lock out with the bar over your ears.

When a rep gets ugly, slow the next one down instead of muscling it. A missed lift costs more time than a deliberate breath. For a deeper look at skill under fatigue, the post on using EMOMs to build skill is a good companion to this one.

Choosing a Weight You Can Finish With

Rx is a target, not a requirement. The right weight is one where you can do the push jerks unbroken in round one and still move them in round five. If you are not sure, scale to something you could complete in the 12-9-6 scheme with a couple of reps in the tank. For many athletes that is 115 to 135 pounds instead of 155, and for newer lifters it can be lighter still. The guide to choosing RX or scaled weights walks through how to decide.

Another honest scale is to keep the weight and cut the rounds to three. You still get the same stimulus for grip and shoulders, and you learn the pacing before you commit to all five. Whichever way you scale, write it down so your retest means something. A garage setup with a decent barbell and bumper plates covers everything you need here.

Final Thoughts

DT is a good first test of whether you can stay patient with a barbell. Pick a weight that lets you finish smoothly, hold a steady round time, and keep the bar close to your body on every lift. Then log it and retest in two months.

If you want something lighter to warm up with or a similar barbell piece for another day, the WOD Builder can build one around your gear, and the Daily 20 is there for short sessions.
